projects.tagline: Windows touchscreen kiosk that links employee badges to a site roster for emergency mustering.
projects.what: A packaged Windows kiosk application that registers employee access badges against a site roster and produces the badge-to-person mapping that emergency mustering depends on. An employee types the first letters of their name, picks themselves from a filtered list and scans a badge, and the ID is written to an encrypted local store; an administrator can export the roster as CSV. It ships as a PyInstaller executable that runs on a tablet at a site entrance with no Python installation.
projects.solves: In an evacuation the key question is who is still inside, which needs a reliable badge-to-person mapping. HR holds names and access control holds badge numbers, and unsupervised registration produces wrong selections, borrowed badges and double registrations, each of which becomes a mustering error. The data is personal and the kiosk has no operator.

versus.incumbents: Clipboard sign-in sheets, full access-control platforms, shared Excel sheets, vendor mustering apps
versus.edge: A single self-contained executable covers the specific enrolment step with no server or network dependency, adding duplicate-person and duplicate-badge guards and atomic encrypted writes. Each kiosk keeps its own encrypted store and exports the roster as CSV, so it stands up at a site entrance on its own.

moves: Debounced scan commit: Badge readers behave like fast keyboards and may or may not send Enter, so each keystroke reschedules a commit 220 ms later while an Enter commits immediately. The kiosk then works with whatever reader is attached.
Scan state machine: The badge field stays disabled until a person is selected and confirmed, so a badge cannot be scanned without first choosing who it belongs to.
Two-sided duplicate detection: The kiosk warns when a person already has a badge and refuses a badge already assigned to someone else, preventing two people from being accounted for by one badge.

Crash-safe storage and packaging: The store is written to a temporary file and atomically renamed, so a power cut cannot corrupt it. Writable data moved to a per-machine user-data location because a one-file bundle unpacks to a temporary directory that is deleted on exit.

Iteration growth: A 360-line first kiosk grew into the current 1,309-line version, almost entirely operator experience: a dark design system, three-panel layout, live activity log, plain-English status prompts and high-DPI handling for tablet screens.

projects.name: Indented BOM Parser and Cost Explorer
projects.tagline: Parses ERP indented bill-of-materials exports into costed trees for cost engineers.
projects.what: A parser and Streamlit dashboard for indented bill-of-materials cost report exports from an ERP. The report encodes hierarchy in a dotted level string with cost-element rows interleaved between component rows. The project rebuilds a real tree, rolls costs up from the leaves, and offers an expandable BOM explorer and a side-by-side cost comparison across product assemblies.
projects.solves: A cost engineer needs to know what an assembly costs to build and where the cost sits, but the export is built to be read on paper: hierarchy is a string, component and cost rows interleave, rollups are absent, and comparing assemblies means paging through several reports. Encodings vary, a metadata header of unpredictable length precedes the data, and rows with embedded commas can shift columns.

versus.incumbents: ERP report viewers, manual Excel manipulation, enterprise costing modules, BI tools on ERP tables
versus.edge: It reads the export the ERP already produces, so no integration or database access is needed, and a parser refined over several iterations handles the format's quirks. Costs roll up from the leaves, so every assembly shows exactly where its cost sits.

moves: Parser iterations: Successive notebook versions each hardened the parser: ordered encoding attempts, content-based header detection instead of a fixed skip count, an explicit terminator scan for the trailing cost block, and a switch from pandas to the standard csv reader to keep columns aligned on rows with embedded commas.
Depth from the indent string: Depth equals the number of dots in the level string, and combined with document order this rebuilds parent-child links with no id join.

Look-ahead aggregation and two-pass rollup: Unindented cost-element rows after each component are summed into that component, then a depth-first pass adds each child's rolled cost to its parent. Interleaved rows are therefore not mistaken for siblings.
Consolidation: A glob-and-concat step stamps each row with its source file and merges several assembly exports into one master table.

projects.name: Manufacturing Quality and Scrap Analytics
projects.tagline: Turns free-text inspection notes and per-unit event logs into quantified defects and rework decision rules.
projects.what: A manufacturing analytics project in two halves. The first converts free-text inspection notes into a quantified defect dataset using a hand-built domain thesaurus. The second reconstructs a per-serial chronological event log across process and test systems and uses it to replace a judgement-based rework loop with numeric decision gates, covered as a sub-project.
projects.solves: A unit that fails its performance test can be reworked, but rework consumes labour and equipment time and much of it fails. A procedure that only caps the number of rework cycles gives no way to tell early which units are worth attempting, and free-text inspection notes otherwise go unaggregated.

versus.incumbents: Procedure decision trees, SPC software, MES dashboards, supervisor judgement, manual log reading
versus.edge: It adds data-derived numeric gates and an explicit sunk-cost analysis where decision trees gate on test results only. A transparent thesaurus extractor turns free-text notes into counts that can be aggregated and audited line by line.

moves: Thesaurus over NLP models: A hand-built synonym map, including deliberate misspellings and shorthand, was chosen over spaCy or transformers because the corpus is short technician notes in a closed domain, and every extracted count stays auditable.
Evidence-driven vocabulary: An out-of-vocabulary scan flagged unmatched comments before the extractor was finalised, so the thesaurus was built from evidence rather than guesses.
Date stripping: Dates are removed before quantity extraction so the numbers inside a date are not read as a defect count.

Defect versus repair split: The first schema counted defects; later schemas split every category into defects found and defects repaired, because three found and all repaired differ from three found and left open. Unmatched quantities fall into an unspecified bucket rather than being dropped.

subs.name: Rework Viability Decision Model
subs.what: A root-cause and decision-analytics study on one manufactured product. It merges process-step dates, performance-test results and a process-count table into a per-serial event log, engineers recovery features from consecutive tests, trains a multi-class XGBoost classifier with SHAP attribution, and distils the result into a procedure with two numeric gates: a viability floor on first-test results and an elapsed-time cutoff for rework.
subs.solves: It answers the day-one question of whether a failed unit is recoverable, previously left to judgement, so units that were never going to pass stop consuming capacity.
subs.edge: Existing decision trees gate on test thresholds and a cycle cap; this adds a data-derived viability floor and an elapsed-time gate while keeping the familiar cap.
moves: Recovery ratio and process DNA: Pairing two tests per serial gives delta performance metrics and a recovery ratio, and collapsing each lot's ordered activity list into one string exposed missing-step route anomalies.

Elapsed time beats test values: A decision tree on the viability outcome split first on rework days rather than on any test measurement, so time already spent predicted failure better than how bad the part was, and that became the time gate. The viability floor is a low-percentile recovery value computed after excluding test-rig zeros, since a naive minimum would be zero.

projects.name: Free-Text Identifier Matching Engines
projects.tagline: Matches unaccounted-for inventory identifiers to free-text shop-floor comments with strict contextual rules.
projects.what: A forensic text-matching project: given identifiers of inventory items that cannot be accounted for, it searches free-text shop-floor comments to find which finished lot consumed them. It contains three successively stricter matching engines, each with its own output file, compared against a baseline result.
projects.solves: When an item is consumed, the technician often writes its number in a comment instead of scanning it, so the comment is the only record. Bare numbers collide with pressure readings and sequence numbers, enumerated lists hide several IDs, formats vary, and a wrong match closes an investigation that should stay open.

versus.incumbents: Ctrl-F on exported comments, barcode trails, MES genealogy reports, off-the-shelf fuzzy matchers
versus.edge: Exact numeric cores with contextual gating, deliberately not fuzzy on the number itself, work from free text where no transaction exists. Each successive engine raises precision by filtering out the numeric coincidences that a baseline search counted as matches, so a surviving match carries real contextual evidence.

moves: IDF rarity gating: A TF-IDF vectorizer with a non-alphanumeric tokenizer measures how distinctive a number is. Rare numbers may match loosely, common numbers need an explicit prefix word, and a suffix blocklist (units and process words such as psi, deg and mm) rejects measurements.

Sticky-list expansion: A regex expands enumerated forms so one comment yields several matches, recovering true positives the prefix rule rejected because only the first number in a list carries the prefix.

Model and year conflict rejection: Each identifier is parsed into year, model code and number, and a hit is rejected if a different model code or year appears in a short window before it. Core extraction skips years so a year is never mistaken for the identifier.
Comparison as the deliverable: Several engines run over the same identifier set and are reported side by side, instead of shipping the first result that looked good.
proof: Three matching engines plus a baseline, each with its own output file
